author: Autodesk
description: This graph demonstrates a classic crown splash using an explicit surface tension solver.
documentation:
## Explicit Surface Tension

### What it does

This graph creates small scale fluid simulations using explicit surface tension.

### Inputs and outputs

This graph is self-contained and generates inputs.

### How it works

- The graph is a classic crown splash setup.  A droplet of fluid is dropped into a "pool" of liquid.

- The liquid simulation is performed using the explicit surface tension solver to produce small scale fluid effects.  The explicit surface tension solver is detailed and more accurate.  

- This graph sets the liquid simulation scale to achieve small scale.  Because Maya works in centimeters, the ***scene_units_in_meters*** is used to setup a smaller simulation.

- The result of the simulation is meshed, shaded and rendered.  A cache can be used to write the output to disk.

_notes.text:
# Resolution:
 - Low:  0.08
 - High: 0.04


This controls the resolution of the entire simulation, you can make this value bigger to get a faster, less accurate simulation for testing purposes.

This graph defaults to the low resolution.
This is set to a lower value to simulate the smaller scale of the fluids.
***surface_tension*** is needed for small-scale fluids.  The simulation can be run without it, but to get small surface features (droplets etc) surface tension must be calculated.

The file_cache compound will save the simulation data out to disk, it is set to *write_state_mode*.  This means the simulation will act as a "passthrough" until this graph is run with "Batch Execute" from the ***Edit*** menu in the Bifrost pane.

When running the simulation at production resolution it is ideal to cache out the simulation data before rendering, as typically the render will take longer than the simulation and can be easily resumed (unlike the simulation)

We are keeping Maya at 24 fps and modifying our simulation speed to emulate running at a higher fps (400) to capture the effect at a reasonable temporal scale. The simulation speed is computed as 24/400.
